subcards.title: Jammu & Kashmir: Art 370 and after
subcards.summary: How J&K's special status under Art 370 ended, and what came after.
at_a_glance: Art 370, called a 'temporary' provision, placed in Part XXI of the Constitution
Two Presidential Orders: C.O. 272 (Constitution Order 272) on 5 August 2019 and C.O. 273 on 6 August 2019
A Constitution Amendment under Art 368 (the normal amendment procedure)
Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 created two Union Territories (J&K and Ladakh) from 31 October 2019
In Re Article 370 case (11 December 2023): a bench of 5 judges upheld the 2019 change; all 5 agreed
114 seats in total. 24 are kept vacant for Pakistan-occupied J&K, so 90 seats are filled by election

As of November 2026, statehood is not restored. The J&K Assembly passed a resolution asking for it on 28 September 2026

sections.heading: Article 370 before 2019: what the special status was

blocks.text: Till 2019, the State of Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) had its own separate constitution and a special status because of Art 370. Art 370 was placed in Part XXI of the Constitution, which deals with 'temporary, transitional and special provisions'; Art 370 was called a 'temporary' provision.

blocks.title: Main features of the old special status
head: Feature
What it meant
rows: J&K joined India through the Instrument of Accession (the legal document by which the State joined India). Under it, India got power over only three subjects: Defence, External Affairs and Communications.
Even with special status, J&K was a State listed in the First Schedule and was part of the territory of India under Art 1.
Not all provisions of the Indian Constitution that apply to other States applied to J&K. Only the provisions that the President extended to J&K by a Presidential Order applied there.
Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954
This was the main Presidential Order made under Art 370. It listed which parts of the Indian Constitution applied to J&K, and with what changes (exceptions and modifications).
Residuary powers (power to make laws on subjects not in any of the three lists) were with the J&K State Legislature. For all other States, residuary powers are with Parliament.

Art 35A was added to the Constitution by the 1954 Order (not by Parliament). It allowed the J&K Legislature to decide who are 'permanent residents' of the State and to give them special rights, for example in jobs and owning land. It ended along with Art 370 in 2019.
J&K had its own separate constitution and its own State laws. For example, it had its own J&K Right to Information Act, 2009 instead of the central RTI Act.

blocks.text: For special provisions for other States (Art 371 to Art 371J), see the card 'Special provisions for some States'

sections.heading: August 2019: how Article 370 was ended

blocks.text: Art 370 was not removed by a Constitution Amendment under Art 368. Instead, it was made inoperative (no longer working) by two Presidential Orders issued under Art 370 itself.

items.what: C.O. 272 (Constitution Order 272): The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019
items.detail: Issued under Art 370(1). It replaced the 1954 Order and applied ALL provisions of the Indian Constitution to J&K. It also changed Art 367 (the clause that explains how words in the Constitution are to be read). Because of this change, the words 'Constituent Assembly of the State' in Art 370(3) were to be read as 'Legislative Assembly of the State'. This mattered because the J&K Constituent Assembly had been dissolved in 1957.

items.what: Parliament passes the resolution (Rajya Sabha 5 August, Lok Sabha 6 August)
items.detail: Art 370(3) needed a recommendation from the State. J&K was under President's Rule (Art 356), so there was no State Assembly; Parliament's resolution was used in place of the State Assembly's recommendation.
The President declared that, from 6 August 2019, all clauses of Art 370 stop operating, except a few words that remain.

items.what: Parliament passes the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019
items.detail: The Act came into force later, on 31 October 2019.

blocks.title: Result
items: J&K no longer has a separate constitution. India now has ONE Constitution for the Centre, all States and all Union Territories (UTs).
Art 35A also ended.
Central (all-India) laws now apply in J&K. For example, the central Right to Information Act, 2005 applies; the old J&K RTI Act, 2009 was repealed (cancelled) by the Reorganisation Act.

sections.heading: J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019: two Union Territories

head: Union Territory
Area
Legislature?
rows: All districts of the old State, except Kargil and Leh
Yes. It has an elected Legislative Assembly, like the UT of Puducherry

items: Date the Act came into force: 31 October 2019.
The J&K Legislative Council (the old upper house of the State) was abolished by this Act.
The UT of J&K is headed by a Lieutenant Governor (LG).

blocks.text: For Ladakh and other UTs, see the card 'Union Territories'

sections.heading: In Re Article 370 judgment (11 December 2023)

blocks.title: The bench
head: Item
Detail
rows: 5-judge Constitution Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) D.Y. Chandrachud, with Justices Sanjay Kishan Kaul, Sanjiv Khanna, B.R. Gavai and Surya Kant

3 separate judgments were written: one by the CJI (for himself, Justice Gavai and Justice Surya Kant), one by Justice Kaul and one by Justice Khanna. All three reached the same result, so the decision was unanimous.

blocks.title: What the Court held
head: Point
Held
rows: Art 370 was a temporary provision. It was an interim (stop-gap) arrangement made because of war conditions in the State at that time.
J&K did not keep any internal sovereignty (supreme power of its own) after joining India. It is an integral part of India, as shown by Art 1 and Art 370.
Valid. The President had the power to declare Art 370 inoperative even after the J&K Constituent Assembly was dissolved in 1957.
C.O. 272: applying the whole Constitution to J&K
Valid. The President could do this under Art 370(1)(d) even without the State Government's agreement.
Invalid. Art 367 only explains how words are to be read; it cannot be used to amend Art 370. Doing so would avoid the proper amendment procedure under Art 368.
Making Ladakh a Union Territory was upheld as valid.

The Court did NOT decide whether Parliament can turn a State into a UT; it left this question open. It did so because the Centre (through the Solicitor General) promised that statehood would be restored. The Court directed that statehood be restored 'at the earliest and as soon as possible', but set NO fixed deadline.
The Election Commission was directed to hold Assembly elections by 30 September 2024.
Justice Kaul, in his separate judgment, suggested a 'truth and reconciliation' commission to look into human rights violations since the 1980s.

sections.heading: Elections 2024 and the statehood question (as of Nov 2026)

items.detail: This was the first Assembly election since 2014, and the first after Art 370 ended.
National Conference 42, BJP 29, Congress 6, PDP 3.

items.what: Omar Abdullah (National Conference) sworn in as Chief Minister
Assembly resolution asking to restore special status and constitutional guarantees
Assembly resolution for 'immediate restoration of full Statehood'
items.detail: Moved by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. BJP members walked out.

items: As of November 2026, J&K is still a Union Territory with a legislature. No Bill to restore statehood has been found in Parliament.
A resolution of the J&K Assembly is only a demand; it does not change anything by itself. Only Parliament can change J&K's status, by making a law under Art 3 and Art 4.

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: Art 370 was ended by Presidential Orders issued under Art 370 itself (C.O. 272 and C.O. 273). It was NOT ended by an amendment under Art 368, by an ordinance or by an order under Art 356.
In the old State of J&K, residuary powers were with the State Legislature, not with Parliament.
The Reorganisation Act came into force on 31 October 2019, not on 5 August 2019.
The Supreme Court in 2023 upheld the change but set NO six-month (or any) deadline for statehood. Only the elections had a deadline: 30 September 2024.
Assembly: 114 seats, minus 24 kept vacant for the Pakistan-occupied area, gives 90 elected seats.
2022 delimitation: Kashmir has 47 seats, more than Jammu's 43. 9 seats were reserved for STs for the first time. There are 5 Lok Sabha seats, each with 18 Assembly seats.
The 2020 Delimitation Commission did delimitation for J&K only, because the four north-eastern States were dropped from its work in 2021.
The 2024 Scheduled Tribes Bill amended the 1989 J&K Scheduled Tribes Order. Separately: today the central RTI Act, 2005 applies in J&K.

blocks.title: Minimum size of the Assembly (normal rule vs special rule)
items: Normal rule (Art 170): a State Legislative Assembly must have at least 60 and at most 500 members.
Special lower minimums: Nagaland at least 46 (Art 371A); Mizoram at least 40 (Art 371G); Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa at least 30 each (Art 371F, 371H, 371-I).

sections.heading: Nagaland, Assam and Manipur (Art 371A, 371B, 371C)

blocks.title: Nagaland (Art 371A, added by the 13th Amendment 1962)
items: Nagaland was formed out of the Naga Hills and Tuensang area by the State of Nagaland Act 1962, but it became a State only from 1 December 1963.

An Act of Parliament on these four matters does not apply to Nagaland unless the Nagaland Legislative Assembly passes a resolution accepting it: (1) religious or social practices of the Nagas; (2) Naga customary law and procedure; (3) civil and criminal justice decided by Naga customary law; (4) ownership and transfer of land and its resources.
This protection covers ONLY those four matters. Other Acts of Parliament apply to Nagaland normally. Boundaries of Nagaland are NOT in this list.

The Governor has special responsibility for law and order as long as internal trouble by hostile Nagas continues. He consults the Council of Ministers, but then acts on his own judgement (called 'individual judgement'), and that decision is final. This ends when the President directs.

The Governor makes sure that money the Centre gives for a specific purpose is included in the State budget's demand for grants (the request for money placed before the Assembly) for that same purpose.

Tuensang district has a regional council of 35 members, with the Deputy Commissioner as chairman. For 10 years (or longer, if the Governor extends it on the council's advice) three special rules apply: the Governor runs Tuensang; there is a Minister for Tuensang affairs; and Tuensang's members of the Assembly are elected by the regional council, not directly by the people.

blocks.title: Assam (Art 371B, added by the 22nd Amendment 1969)
items: The President may create a committee of the Assam Legislative Assembly made up of members elected from the Tribal Areas of Assam (and other members he specifies).
Tribal Areas of Assam are listed in the Sixth Schedule: North Cachar Hills, Karbi Anglong and Bodoland Territorial Areas District.

blocks.text: → see Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas (Sixth Schedule)

blocks.title: Manipur (Art 371C, added by the 27th Amendment 1971)
items: The President may create a committee of the Manipur Legislative Assembly made up of members elected from the Hill Areas. 'Hill Areas' are areas the President declares by order.
The President may make the Governor specially responsible for the proper working of this Hill Areas Committee.
The Governor sends a yearly report to the President on how the Hill Areas are run.
The Central Government can give directions to the State Government on running the Hill Areas.

sections.heading: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (Art 371D and 371E)

blocks.text: Art 371D and Art 371E were both added by the 32nd Amendment Act 1973 (in force from 1 July 1974). The same amendment took Andhra Pradesh out of Art 371. Art 371D was extended to Telangana by Section 97 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014; its heading now reads 'the State of Andhra Pradesh or the State of Telangana'.

blocks.title: What Art 371D allows the President to do
head: Power
Meaning in simple words
rows: Give people of different parts of the State fair and equal chances in government jobs and in education; different rules can be made for different parts.
Ask the State to group civil posts into local cadres (posts filled only from one area), and provide direct recruitment to them.
Decide which part of the State counts as the 'local area' for admission to an educational institution.
Decide how much preference or reservation locals get in direct recruitment and in admissions.

Set up a State Administrative Tribunal for disputes on appointment, allotment and promotion to civil posts. It works outside the High Court's control; no court except the Supreme Court can hear those matters. Set up by the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal Order 1975.
The President may abolish the tribunal by order when he feels it is no longer needed.

blocks.title: Art 371E — Central University
items: Parliament may by law set up a Central University in the State of Andhra Pradesh. (This became the University of Hyderabad.)
The university set up under Art 371E is listed in the Union List of the Seventh Schedule (the 32nd Amendment amended the Seventh Schedule for this).
Art 371E was NOT amended in 2014 to mention Telangana; only Art 371D was.

items.detail: Mulki Rules were old Hyderabad State rules that kept government jobs in Telangana for 'mulkis' (local residents). The Regional Committee looked after Telangana's interests in the Assembly. Court cases on the Mulki Rules led to the Jai Andhra movement of 1972.

A political settlement agreed by national and State leaders. Its six points were: faster development of backward areas; local preference in admissions and a Central University at Hyderabad; local preference in some direct recruitment with local cadres; a high-power administrative tribunal; a constitutional amendment to give it legal backing and avoid court cases; Mulki Rules and Regional Committee no longer needed.
Inserted Art 371D and 371E to give the Six-Point Formula constitutional force.

Full name: Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisation of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 1975. It grouped the 23 districts of the then united Andhra Pradesh into six zones (Zones I to IV in the Andhra and Rayalaseema regions, Zones V and VI in Telangana) and set up local cadres with reservation for local candidates. The State notified it by G.O.Ms. No. 674 on 20 Oct 1975.
Set up the Administrative Tribunal under Art 371D.

G.O.Ms. No. 610, issued by the Andhra Pradesh Government on 30 December 1985, to correct jobs wrongly filled against the zonal rules of the 1975 Presidential Order. It ordered non-local employees wrongly placed in Telangana's Zones V and VI to be sent back to their own zones.
The Supreme Court struck down the proviso (an extra condition added to a clause) in clause (5) of Art 371D.
Section 97 of this Act extended Art 371D to Telangana.

The President approved a new zonal system for Telangana, notified on 30 Aug 2018. It has 7 zones in 2 multi-zones, and 95% of posts are kept for local candidates. It was amended in April 2021 to fit Telangana's new districts.

Petitioners told the Andhra Pradesh High Court that the government orders (G.O.s) to create 13 new districts (taking the State from 13 to 26 districts) violated Art 371D. On 14 March 2022 a bench of Chief Justice Prashant Kumar Mishra and Justice M. Satyanarayana Murthy refused to give interim orders (a temporary stop while the case is heard), because only a draft notification had been issued.

items.what: New Andhra Pradesh Presidential Order (as of Nov 2026)
items.detail: Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisation of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 2025. The President issued it on 15 December 2025 (Ministry of Home Affairs notification S.O. 5777(E)). The State published it by G.O.Ms. No. 45 on 20 April 2026. It creates 6 zones grouped into 2 multi-zones (Zones I to III in Multi-zone I, Zones IV to VI in Multi-zone II). Its schedule lists the 26 districts that existed when it was made; Andhra Pradesh now has 28 districts after Polavaram and Markapuram were added. 95% of posts filled by direct recruitment are reserved for local candidates. It replaces the 1975 Order for Andhra Pradesh.

blocks.title: Key case
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: P. Sambamurthy vs State of Andhra Pradesh (1986)
The proviso (extra condition) to clause (5) of Art 371D let the State Government change or cancel the Administrative Tribunal's orders. The Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional.

It is one of the few cases where part of a constitutional amendment (the 32nd) was struck down. Reason: a tribunal that takes the place of the High Court must be independent, so the State Government cannot overrule it.

sections.heading: Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa (Art 371F to 371-I)

items.detail: Made Sikkim an 'associate state' (linked to India but not a full State). Added Art 2A and a 10th Schedule setting out the terms of this link.
People voted to end the Chogyal (king) and join India fully.
Made Sikkim a full State (22nd State). Added Art 371F. Removed Art 2A and that 10th Schedule.

blocks.title: Sikkim (Art 371F)
items: The Sikkim Assembly has at least 30 members.
Sikkim gets one Lok Sabha seat; the whole State is one parliamentary constituency.
To protect different sections of Sikkim's people, Parliament may fix seats in the Assembly that only those sections can contest, and draw constituencies for them.
The Governor has special responsibility for peace and for fair social and economic progress of all sections; he acts in his discretion, subject to the President's directions.
The President can extend to Sikkim any law in force in any other State (with changes).

Sangha seat: one Assembly seat reserved for the Sangha (Buddhist monks and nuns). Only registered monks and nuns of Sikkim's monasteries can vote for this seat, and only they can contest it. It has NO fixed geographical boundary.

blocks.title: Mizoram (Art 371G, 53rd Amendment 1986)
items: Mizoram became a State on 20 February 1987 under the State of Mizoram Act 1986 (after the Mizoram Peace Accord of 1986).

Acts of Parliament on Mizo religious or social practices, Mizo customary law and procedure, justice by Mizo customary law, and ownership and transfer of land do not apply unless the Mizoram Assembly agrees.
Mizoram Assembly has at least 40 members.

blocks.title: Arunachal Pradesh (Art 371H, 55th Amendment 1986)
items: Became a State on 20 February 1987 under the State of Arunachal Pradesh Act 1986.
The Governor has special responsibility for law and order. He consults the Council of Ministers, but his own judgement ('individual judgement') is final. This ends when the President directs.
Arunachal Pradesh Assembly has at least 30 members.

blocks.title: Goa (Art 371-I, 56th Amendment 1987)
items: Goa became a State on 30 May 1987 under the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act 1987.
Art 371-I has only one rule: the Goa Assembly has at least 30 members.
Why a constitutional amendment was needed: Art 170 normally needs at least 60 members, so a smaller Goa Assembly needed a special Article.

The Centre's power to levy service tax (Art 268A) came from the 88th Amendment 2003, not the 98th.

head: State
Governor's special responsibility
Article

blocks.note: Madhya Pradesh is different: the Constitution (Art 164) requires a Minister for Tribal Welfare in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha. This is not a Governor's special responsibility.

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: 371A is Nagaland, 371B is Assam (not the reverse). 371C Manipur, 371F Sikkim, 371G Mizoram, 371H Arunachal Pradesh.
Art 371A protects only four matters (religion, customary law, justice by customary law, land). It does not stop every Act of Parliament, and it does not cover boundaries.
Six-Point Formula (1973) got legal backing through the 32nd Amendment, not the 31st, 33rd or 35th.
Art 371D was extended to Telangana in 2014; Art 371E (Central University) still names only Andhra Pradesh.

The 35th Amendment 1974 made Sikkim an associate state (it added Art 2A and the old 10th Schedule). The 36th Amendment 1975 made Sikkim a full State and added Art 371F. Today's 10th Schedule (anti-defection law) was added later by the 52nd Amendment 1985; it is a different schedule.
Sangha seat (Sikkim): only monks vote and only monks contest; it has no geographical boundary.
Minimum Assembly size: Goa, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh at least 30; Mizoram at least 40; Nagaland at least 46; all other States at least 60.
Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh both became States on 20 Feb 1987; Goa on 30 May 1987.

subcards.title: Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas
subcards.summary: How the Constitution protects tribal areas through the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
at_a_glance: Part X: Article 244, Article 244A; also Article 339 and Article 275
Scheduled Areas in 10 States (including Andhra Pradesh and Telangana)
Tribal Areas in 4 North-East States: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
The President, after consulting the Governor
Up to 20 members; three-fourths of them must be Scheduled Tribe (ST) members of the State Legislative Assembly
10 in total; each district council normally has 30 members (26 elected, 4 nominated by the Governor)
Parliament can amend them by a simple majority (an ordinary law); such a law is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368
Samatha case (1997): the Supreme Court held that land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to non-tribal private companies for mining

sections.heading: Basics: Article 244 and the two Schedules

blocks.text: Purpose of both Schedules: to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes (STs) — their land, culture, self-rule and freedom from exploitation. Scheduled Tribes mainly live in these Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas.

blocks.title: Articles to remember
head: Article
What it says
rows: The Fifth Schedule applies to the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
The Sixth Schedule applies to the administration of Tribal Areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

Parliament may form an autonomous State made of certain tribal areas inside Assam, with its own local legislature, Council of Ministers, or both. Added by the 22nd Amendment Act, 1969 (this paved the way for Meghalaya).

Control of the Union over the administration of Scheduled Areas and the welfare of STs. The Union can give directions to a State on schemes for ST welfare, and the President appoints a commission to report on the administration of Scheduled Areas.

Grants-in-aid (money given by the Union to a State to help it) for States that need help. These include special grants for the welfare of STs and for better administration of Scheduled Areas, and also of the tribal areas of Assam. They are given on the Finance Commission's recommendation.

blocks.title: Simple picture
items: Fifth Schedule deals with 'Scheduled Areas' — tribal areas in States other than the 4 North-East States. It has been called 'a constitution within a constitution'.

Sixth Schedule deals with 'Tribal Areas' — only in 4 North-East States. Its focus is tribal self-rule through autonomous district councils, because many of these communities ruled themselves until the British took over in the 19th century.

blocks.text: see Financial relations for Article 275 grants in general

sections.heading: Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas

blocks.text: 10 States have Scheduled Areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan. (Assam is NOT one of them — it is under the Sixth Schedule.)

blocks.title: Main features
head: Feature
Rule
rows: The President declares an area a Scheduled Area by an Order. The President can also increase or decrease it, change its boundary, cancel it, or re-declare it — after consulting the Governor of that State.
Criteria for declaring (not written in the Constitution, but well established in practice)

1. Most people are tribal (preponderance of tribal population). 2. The area is compact and of reasonable size. 3. It is a workable administrative unit such as a District, Block or Taluk. 4. It is economically backward compared to nearby areas.
The largest unit that can form a Scheduled Area is a whole District; the smallest is a cluster of villages inside a Block (asked in UPSC 2023).

The State's executive power still covers its Scheduled Areas — the State does NOT lose it. The Union can only give directions to the State about these areas; it cannot take over their whole administration.
The Governor (not the Chief Minister) sends a report on the administration of Scheduled Areas to the President — every year, or whenever the President asks.

Every State with Scheduled Areas must set up a Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) to advise on the welfare and advancement of STs. Up to 20 members; three-fourths of them must be ST members of the State Legislative Assembly. A State with STs but no Scheduled Areas sets up a TAC only if the President directs.

The Governor can direct, by public notification, that any Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, or shall apply with changes (exceptions and modifications).
Regulations (special rules made by the Governor)

The Governor makes regulations for the peace and good government of a Scheduled Area, after consulting the TAC. These regulations can: stop or limit transfer of land by or among STs; regulate allotment of land to STs; regulate money-lending to STs; repeal or amend an Act of Parliament or of the State Legislature that applies to the area. Every such regulation needs the President's assent.

blocks.text: Main effect of declaring an area 'Scheduled': tribal land is protected — it cannot easily be transferred to non-tribals. Declaring it does NOT create a local self-governing body, does NOT make it a Union Territory, and does NOT make the State a 'Special Category State'.
see 73rd Amendment for PESA 1996 (panchayats in Scheduled Areas) and Article 243M exemptions

sections.heading: Sixth Schedule: Tribal Areas of the North-East

blocks.title: Main features
head: Feature
Rule
rows: The tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram are made 'autonomous districts' (districts with self-rule). They are still under the executive authority of the State — they are NOT outside the State Legislature or the State Government.
The Governor (not the President) can organise and reorganise autonomous districts: increase or decrease their area, change names, fix boundaries.

If an autonomous district has different tribes, the Governor can divide it into autonomous regions. So an autonomous region is a smaller self-ruling unit inside an autonomous district. Each region has its own regional council.

30 members: 26 elected by adult franchise (every adult votes) and 4 nominated by the Governor. Elected members serve 5 years (unless the council is dissolved earlier); nominated members serve at the pleasure of the Governor (as long as the Governor wishes).

District and regional councils can make laws on listed subjects: land, forests, canal water, shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance of property, marriage and divorce, social customs, etc. These laws need the Governor's assent.

Councils can set up village councils or courts to try suits and cases between tribals, and hear appeals from them. The High Court's jurisdiction (power) over these cases is NOT removed — the Governor specifies how far it extends.

A district council can set up or manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets, ferries, fisheries, roads, etc. It can regulate money-lending and trading by non-tribals (with the Governor's assent). Councils can assess and collect land revenue and levy certain taxes.

Acts of Parliament or of the State Legislature may be stopped from applying to these areas, or applied with changes. Who decides this: in Assam, the Governor (for both Central and State Acts). In Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, the President decides for Acts of Parliament and the Governor for State Acts.
The Governor can appoint a commission to inquire into the administration of autonomous districts or regions, and can dissolve a district or regional council on that commission's recommendation.

blocks.title: The 10 autonomous districts (as per Laxmikanth; names verified as of Nov 2026)
head: State

Khasi Hills District; Jaintia Hills District; Garo Hills District

blocks.note: Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur are NOT under the Sixth Schedule.

items: The 49th Amendment Act, 1984 gave constitutional status (by bringing it under the Sixth Schedule) to the Autonomous District Council in Tripura.
There is no rule that STs must be 40% of a State's population for the Sixth Schedule to apply — it applies to the 4 named States.

Bodoland is an exception to the 30-member rule: the Bodoland Territorial Council has 46 members — 40 elected and 6 nominated by the Governor of Assam. Under the Bodo Peace Accord of 27 January 2020, the area is now called the Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR); Laxmikanth's list still uses the older name 'Bodoland Territorial Areas District'.

blocks.title: Commissions and committees on STs (in order)

items.detail: Committee on Special Multipurpose Tribal Blocks (its report came out in 1960)
First Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes Commission. Under Article 339, the President must appoint such a commission 10 years after the Constitution began (1950), and may appoint one at any time.
Set up by the Ministry of Education and Social Welfare. It gave the Tribal Sub-Plan strategy (a separate share of plan funds for tribal areas).
Second Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes Commission

blocks.title: Case
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Samatha case (1997) — Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 11 July 1997
Government, tribal and forest land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to non-tribals or private companies for mining. Such leases are void (null) because they violate the Fifth Schedule.
The case arose from the agency (tribal) areas of Andhra Pradesh. Shows the Fifth Schedule protects tribal land from transfer to non-tribals.

blocks.title: Related laws
head: Law
Key point
rows: PESA Act, 1996 (Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act)
Extends the panchayat system (Part IX) to Fifth Schedule areas, with changes; made on the recommendation of the Bhuria Committee (1991). Details are in the 73rd Amendment card.
Forest Rights Act, 2006 (Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act)
Gives rights to forest-dwelling STs and other traditional forest dwellers. The right to land under it is a legal (statutory) right, NOT a Fundamental Right.
Constitution (Jammu and Kashmir) Scheduled Tribes Order (Amendment) Act, 2024 (secondary)

Passed by Rajya Sabha on 9 February 2024. It amended the Constitution (Jammu and Kashmir) Scheduled Tribes Order, 1989, adding Gadda Brahmin, Koli, Paddari Tribe and Pahari Ethnic Group to the ST list of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.

sections.heading: Scheduled Areas in Andhra Pradesh

items: AP's Scheduled Areas (often called 'agency areas') are under the Fifth Schedule read with Article 244(1) — NOT the Sixth Schedule.
Before the 2022 district reorganisation, they lay in 5 districts: Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, East Godavari and West Godavari.

Alluri Sitharama Raju district was formed on 4 April 2022 with its headquarters at Paderu. It was made from two revenue divisions: Paderu (earlier in Visakhapatnam district) and Rampachodavaram (earlier in East Godavari district). The whole district came under the ITDA (Integrated Tribal Development Agency).

Polavaram district was formed on 31 December 2025 (G.O. Ms. No. 517), with its headquarters at Rampachodavaram. It took 12 mandals out of Alluri Sitharama Raju district: the 8 mandals of the Rampachodavaram revenue division and the 4 mandals of the Chinturu revenue division. With Polavaram and Markapuram, Andhra Pradesh has 28 districts (new map released in April 2026).
The Governor of Andhra Pradesh can stop Acts of Parliament or State Acts from applying to these areas, or apply them with changes, and can make regulations (with the President's assent).
The Samatha case (1997) came from these areas.

sections.heading: Exam traps

items: The President declares and alters Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule); the Governor creates and alters autonomous districts (Sixth Schedule).
Tribes Advisory Council: up to 20 members, three-fourths of them ST members of the State Legislative Assembly. District council: 30 members (26 elected, 4 nominated).
Governor (not the Chief Minister) reports to the President on Scheduled Areas.
Governor's Fifth Schedule regulations need the President's assent; district council laws need the Governor's assent.
Nagaland is NOT in the Sixth Schedule; Assam is NOT in the Fifth Schedule.
The High Court's jurisdiction (power to hear cases) in Sixth Schedule areas is not removed — the Governor specifies how far it extends.
Both Schedules are amended by Parliament by a simple majority; such a law is not an amendment under Article 368.
The State keeps its executive power in Scheduled Areas; the Union can only give directions to the State.
